text: Improvement of Lithium−Sulfur Battery Performance by Porous Carbon Selection and LiFSI/DME Electrolyte Optimization Luna Yoshida, Yukiko Matsui, Minako Deguchi, Takashi Hakari, Masayoshi Watanabe, and Masashi Ishikawa* Cite This: ACS Appl.

Interfaces 2023, 15, 37467−37476 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: High-concentration lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)- imide/1,2-dimethoxyethane (LiFSI/DME) electrolytes are promising candidates for highly reversible lithium−metal anodes.

However, the performance of lithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries with a high concentration of LiFSI/DME declines because LiFSI reacts irreversibly with lithium polysulfide, which is formed during the charge−discharge process of Li−S batteries.

Hence, to apply high-concentration LiFSI/DME to Li−S batteries, we investigated carbon with an appropriate pore size for use in a sulfur composite cathode and optimized the composition of high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

The results showed that the combination of carbon with mesopores of 2−3 nm diameter and 3 M LiFSI in DME/ 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropylether (HFE) (1:1 by vol.) provided a high-rate capability (943 mA h g−1 at a rate of 2 C).
Moreover, the ratio of the 50th discharge capacity to the 2nd discharge capacity (capacity retention) improved from 50.0 to 61.6% with HFE dilution of high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

The improved performance was achieved by suppressing the dissolution of lithium polysulfide, decreasing the viscosity of the electrolyte, and forming a thin solid electrolyte interface on the lithium−metal anode due to HFE dilution.

KEYWORDS: LiFSI, DME, localized high-concentration electrolytes, lithium metal, sulfur, microporous carbon, lithium−sulfur battery ■INTRODUCTION Recently, electricity generated by energy sources that do not emit greenhouse gases such as CO2, wind, and solar power, has been promoted as a global warming countermeasure.1,2 To efficiently utilize clean energy, a high-energy-density storage device is essential.3 Lithium−sulfur (Li−S) batteries with sulfur cathodes and lithium−metal anodes have received attention as high-energy-density storage systems.4 The theoretical specific capacities of sulfur and lithium are 1672 and 3860 mA h g−1, respectively, providing Li−S batteries with twice the volumetric energy density and six times the gravimetric energy density of lithium-ion batteries.5 Therefore, Li−S batteries are ideal storage devices for clean energy sources.
However, the practical application of Li−S batteries faces several challenges.

At the cathode, sulfur reacts with lithium ions to form lithium polysulfide (Li2Sx) during the charge−discharge process.6,7 In particular, Li2Sx (x = 6−8) exhibits high solubility in most organic electrolytes.8,9 The dissolution of Li2Sx causes loss of the active material, redox shuttling, and pollution of the lithium anode, which hinders the stable cycling of Li−S batteries.

To address this problem, Nazar et al. reported a method for confining sulfur in the pores of highly ordered mesoporous carbon.10 The dissolution of Li2Sx into the electrolyte is kinetically suppressed owing to the interaction between the carbon materials and Li2Sx.
Consequently, the Li−S batteries are successfully charged and discharged without a redox shuttle.

However, mesoporous carbons cannot completely inhibit polar Li2Sx dissolution because the carbon surface is generally nonpolar.11 Hence, surface modification of mesoporous carbons with polymers, functional groups, or metal compounds should be applied to impart polarity to the carbon surface.12−15 Lithium−metal anodes also have fundamental problems.
Lithium metal reacts chemically with all electrolytes; therefore, continuous electrolyte decomposition occurs and a thick solid electrolyte interface (SEI) forms on the anode.

This results in a low coulombic efficiency and high cell resistance.16,17 Moreover, the lithium−metal anode undergoes repeated deposition and dissolution during the charge−discharge process, which induces lithium dendrite formation.18 The lithium dendrites Received: May 9, 2023 Accepted: July 18, 2023 Published: July 26, 2023 Research Article www.acsami.org © 2023 American Chemical Society 37467 https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.3c06624 ACS Appl.

can break through the separator and touch the cathode, causing cell ignition and explosion.

Furthermore, the heterogeneous dissolution of lithium dendrites during the discharge process forms dead lithium, which loses its electronic contact with the anode.19 Dead lithium is electrochemically inactive and causes capacity fading.

Various electrolytes and additives have been investigated to suppress the excess decomposition of electrolytes and formation of lithium dendrites.20,21 A high-concentration lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide/1,2-dimethoxyethane (LiFSI/DME) electrolyte has been reported to achieve a stable SEI and dendrite-free lithium−metal anode.22 In particular, a Li/Cu cell with 3−5 M LiFSI/DME showed a high coulombic efficiency.
The application of high-concentration LiFSI/DME in Li−S batteries suppresses electrolyte decomposition and short circuits, thereby improving battery performance.

However, Li2Sx dissolved from the mesoporous carbon−sulfur composite cathode reacts with bis- (fluorosulfonyl)imide (FSI) irreversibly.23 This leads to loss of cathode active material and reduces the coulombic efficiency and capacity of Li−S batteries.24 Carbonate electrolytes that react with Li2Sx irreversibly cannot be used for Li−S batteries; however, we previously reported that Li−S batteries with carbonate electrolytes could be cycled using a microporous carbon−sulfur composite cathode.25 This is because the small pore size (<2 nm) of the microporous carbon suppressed contact between Li2Sx in the micropores and the solvent.26,27 Microporous carbon suppresses Li2Sx dissolution more effectively than mesoporous carbon, and Li−S batteries with carbonate electrolytes exhibit high cycle stability.
These studies suggest that carbon materials with appropriate pore sizes can be used to realize Li−S batteries containing high-concentration LiFSI/DME electrolytes with superior cycling performance.
In this study, we investigated the pore size of carbon materials used in cathodes to achieve high-performance Li−S batteries with high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

Furthermore, we prepared a suitable high-concentration LiFSI/DME electrolyte for use with the micro-mesoporous carbon−sulfur composite cathode and analyzed the effect of the electrolyte on the cathode and anode. 1,1,2,2-Tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3- tetrafluoropropylether (HFE) was used for the electrolyte optimization.

Because HFE is one of the hydrofluoroethers with the lowest lithium-solvating ability,28 dilution with HFE significantly reduces the viscosity of high-concentration LiFSI/ DME while maintaining the locally high concentration of the LiFSI/DME electrolyte.29 Moreover, HFE suppresses the side reaction between Li2Sx and lithium−metal anodes, and improves the deposition morphology of lithium−metal anodes;30 thus, HFE is a promising solvent for electrolyte optimization.

We believe that our systematic evaluation of the physical and chemical characteristics of the carbon materials, electrolyte conditions, and effects of each electrolyte component on the cathode and anode will guide the design of high-performance Li−S batteries. ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Preparation of Porous Carbon−Sulfur Composites.
Three commercial porous carbons with different pore size distributions (Cmicro, Cmicro−meso, and Cmeso) were used as purchased.

Porous carbon−sulfur composites (Cmicro−S, Cmicro−meso−S, and Cmeso−S) were prepared using the same procedure described in a previous study.31 Additional details are provided in the Supporting Information.
Characterization of Materials.
The shapes and surfaces of the porous carbon samples were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FlexSEM 1000 II, Hitachi High-Technologies Co.).
The accelerating voltage and working distance were set to 5.00 kV and 5 mm, respectively.
The particle size distribution of the porous carbon samples was analyzed using a laser scattering particle size distribution analyzer (LA-950, HORIBA, Ltd.).
Pore structures of porous carbons were investigated by the N2 adsorption/desorption method using a fully automatic gas adsorption amount measuring device (autosorb iQ, Anton Paar Japan Co.).
The specific surface area and pore volume distribution were calculated using Brunauer− Emmett−Teller (BET) and quenched solid density functional theory (QSDFT) methods, respectively.
The functional groups on the porous carbon surfaces were analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, JPS-9010MC, JEOL Co.).
Mg Kα radiation was used as the X-ray source.
The spectra were corrected such that the adventitious carbon peak in the C 1s spectrum was at 284.8 eV.
Sulfur in the pores or on the surface of porous carbons was investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Ultima IV, Rigaku Co.) with Cu Kα radiation as the X-ray source.
The accelerating voltage was 40 kV and the tube current was 40 mA.
The maximum peak intensities of all the XRD spectra were standardized to the same value.
The sulfur content of the porous carbon−sulfur composites was measured using thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA, DTG-60AH, Shimadzu Co.).
The rate of temperature increase was set to 5 °C min−1, and the carrier gas was Ar.
The elemental distribution of the porous carbon−sulfur composites was investigated using energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX, FlexSEM 1000 II, Hitachi High- Technologies Co.).
The accelerating voltage was set to 15.0 kV.

The viscosity and ionic conductivity of various electrolytes was investigated at 25 °C using a viscometer (VM-10A, Sekonic Co.) and an impedance analyzer (VMP-300, Bio-Logic Science Instruments Ltd.), respectively.
The suppression effect of the electrolytes on Li2Sx dissolution was measured using ultraviolet−visible absorption (UV− vis) spectroscopy.
Deuterium and halogen light sources were used for measurement (DH-2000-BAL, Ocean Optics).
The effect of the electrolyte on the lithium anode surface was analyzed using SEM and XPS (PHI Quantes, ULVAC-PHI, Inc.).
The accelerating voltage for SEM was set to 15.0 kV.
The X-ray source for XPS was Al Kα radiation.
The spectra of the top surface were corrected such that the adventitious carbon peak in the C 1s spectrum was at 284.8 eV.
After etching, the spectra were corrected such that the peak ascribed to LiF in the F 1s spectrum was at 685 eV.
The lithium anode was removed from the charged−discharged cells after 10 cycles, washed with HFE, and analyzed.
All the experiments were performed under Ar or vacuum.
Preparation of Electrolytes.
LiFSI was added to DME and stirred overnight to prepare 3, 3.6, and 4 M LiFSI (Nippon Shokubai Co., Ltd.)/DME (Kishida Chemical Co., Ltd.).
To prepare electrolytes22 consisting of the two solvents, DME was mixed with HFE (Daikin Industries, Ltd.) in a volume ratio of 1:1.
The salt concentration of the co-solvent was 3 M (3 M LiFSI in DME/ HFE).
The molar ratio of LiFSI/DME/HFE in the 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE solution was 1:1.2:0.83.
All operations were performed in an Ar-filled glovebox.
Electrochemical Measurements.
The cathodes with Cmicro−S, Cmicro−meso−S, or Cmeso−S were prepared using the same procedure described in a previous study,31 and details are provided in the Supporting Information.
The lithium−metal anode was prepared by punching out Li foil (200 μm, Honjo Metal Co., Ltd.) with a 13 mm diameter.
The anode’s surface area was 1.33 cm2.
Cells adopting a porous carbon−sulfur composite cathode, lithium−metal anode, and electrolyte were assembled in an Ar-filled glovebox.
Two microporous polypropylene membranes were used to prevent short circuits.
The separator’s surface area was 2.54 cm2.
The electrolyte used for each Li−S battery was fixed at 52.0 μL.
Constant current charge−discharge tests were conducted using a battery tester (BTS-2004H, Nagano Co., Ltd.).

The specific capacity was calculated based on the mass of sulfur in the cathode. ■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Characterization of Porous Carbons.
Various measurements were performed to reveal the physical and chemical structures of porous carbon materials.
The particle shapes and surfaces of the porous carbons were observed by SEM (Figure 1a).
Cmicro and Cmeso exhibited rugged shapes and rough surfaces, respectively.
Cmicro−meso had a rounded shape and smooth surface.
Particle size distributions were measured to determine the exact particle size of the porous carbons.
The median diameters of Cmicro, Cmicro−meso, and Cmeso were 3.49, 2.52, and 49.8 μm, respectively (Figure S1).

A small particle size increases the surface area of porous carbon−sulfur composite cathodes and shortens the electronic and ionic conductive paths, which improves the discharge capacity and rate capability.32−35 N2 adsorption/desorption measurements were performed to investigate the pore structures of the porous carbons; Figure 1b shows the isotherms.

According to IUPAC classification, the isotherms of Cmicro, Cmicro−meso, and Cmeso are classified as type I(a), type I(b), and type IV(a), respectively.36 Therefore, Cmicro mainly contains micropores, Cmicro−meso contains micropores with a narrow range of slight mesopores, and Cmeso mainly contains mesopores.
Figure 1c shows the pore size distributions of the porous carbon materials.
Cmicro has a pore diameter of 2 nm or less and is therefore a typical microporous carbon.
Although Cmicro−meso mainly has micropores, there are a small number of mesopores of 2 nm or more and 3 nm or less.
Cmeso has a pore diameter of 2 nm or more and 50 nm or less; therefore, it is a typical mesoporous carbon.
The specific surface areas and pore volumes of the porous carbon samples were calculated from the isotherms (Table 1).
The pore diameter was correlated with the specific surface area and pore volume.
Carbon with a large pore volume can confine a large amount of sulfur; thus, Cmicro−meso or Cmeso could offer the advantage of cell energy density over Cmicro.
XPS measurements were performed to investigate the surface composition of the porous carbons.
Figure S2 shows wide-scan XPS spectra.
All the porous carbons contained only carbon and oxygen.
Narrow-scan XPS was used to analyze the surfaces in detail (Figure 1d,e).

The C 1s spectra of all porous carbons had peaks around 284.6 and 288.6 eV, which were attributed to C−C and −COO bonds, respectively.37 Moreover, the peaks around 532.9 eV in the O 1s spectra were ascribed to C−O and CO bonds in the porous carbons.38 The surface composition ratios, calculated from the peak areas of the C 1s and O 1s spectra (Table 1), revealed that Cmicro had the highest number of oxygen functional groups and Cmeso had the lowest number of oxygen-containing functional groups among all carbon materials.

Characterization of Porous Carbon−Sulfur Composites.
The sulfur content of the porous carbon−sulfur composites was measured using TGA and DTA (Figures 2 and S3).
Sulfur generally evaporates at around 155 °C.
Thus, the weight loss observed in TGA curves around 155 °C was consistent with the sulfur content of porous carbon−sulfur composites.
The sulfur contents of Cmicro−S, Cmicro−meso−S, and Cmeso−S were 21.4, 51.2, and 60.0 wt %, respectively.

However, the TGA curves of porous carbon−sulfur composites showed a weight loss onset temperature slightly higher than 155 °C, indicating that additional energy was needed for the evaporation of sulfur in the micropores.
EDX measurements were carried out to obtain elemental mappings of the porous carbon−sulfur composites (Figure S4).
All the porous carbon−sulfur composites consisted of carbon, oxygen, and sulfur.
All the elements were uniformly distributed.
Table S1 shows the weight ratios of the elements obtained from EDX mapping, and the trend is consistent with that of XPS and TGA.
The crystallinity of microporous carbon−sulfur composites measured using XRD is discussed in the Supporting Information (Figure S5).
Electrochemical Performances of Porous Carbon−Sulfur Composite Cathodes with 3 M LiFSI/DME.
Galvanostatic charge−discharge measurements were performed to investigate the effect of the pore structure of porous carbons on the performance of Li−S batteries with 3 M LiFSI/DME.
Figure 3a shows the charge−discharge curves of the Li−S batteries at the 1st and 50th cycles.
Cmicro−S showed only one plateau at low potential (∼1.6−1.9 V).
This plateau was attributed to the formation of Li2Sx (x = 1, 2).14 In contrast, Cmicro−meso−S and Cmeso−S exhibited a plateau at a high potential (∼2.0 V) in addition to a low-potential plateau.
The high-potential plateau was attributed to the reduction of sulfur to Li2Sx (x = 4−8).14 Figure 3b shows the cycle plots of the Li−S batteries.
Cmicro−S had high capacity retention (83.4%), which was calculated by dividing the discharge capacity at the 50th cycle (934.5 mA h g−1) by the discharge capacity at the 2nd cycle (1121 mA h g−1).
Furthermore, Cmicro−S showed high coulombic efficiency (average 99.4%).

This stable cycle performance could be due to the suppression of Li2Sx dissolution, which causes loss of the cathode active material and redox shuttling for two reasons: (i) micropores suppress the formation of Li2Sx (x = 4−8) and42 (ii) the decomposition products of the electrolyte formed by charging and discharging completely cover the pores, which inhibits contact between the electrolyte solvent and the cathode active material.27 The coulombic efficiency of Cmeso−S significantly exceeded 100% at the 11th cycle, and the Li−S battery with the Cmeso−S cathode did not reach the charge cut-off voltage at the 14th cycle.

Qian and Fu reported that the molar ratio of Li+ to DME in 3 M LiFSI/DME is 1:2.2, and Li+ is coordinated with five oxygen atoms of FSI−and DME molecules.22,43 From this electrolyte composition, they suggested that it contained uncoordinated DME molecules.

In the case of Cmeso−S, Li2Sx (x = 6−8) would be able to dissolve in the uncoordinated DME of the 3 M LiFSI/DME electrolyte because Cmeso has mainly mesopores, from which Li2Sx dissolves into uncoordinated DME easily.
The dissolved Li2Sx in the electrolyte removed from the cycled cell were confirmed by UV−vis spectroscopy (Figure S6).
Cmeso−S and Cmicro−meso−S had a peak ascribed to Sx 2−at 350−500 nm; the peak intensity of Cmeso−S was approximately four times higher than that of Cmicro−meso−S.

In addition, the Sx 2−peak was not observed in the Cmicro−S spectrum.24,44 Thus, Cmeso−S could not reach the cut-off voltage owing to the redox shuttle, pollution of the lithium anode, and the irreversible reaction between dissolved Li2Sx and LiFSI.23 The cell with Cmicro−meso−S was discharged and charged with a capacity decay.

Electrochemical performances of Cmicro−meso−S cathode with various concentrations of LiFSI/DME electrolytes.
The Cmicro−S/Li battery with 3 M LiFSI/DME exhibited high cycle stability owing to the suppression of Li2Sx dissolution.
However, the sulfur content of Cmicro−S was only 21.4 wt %, which is disadvantageous in terms of energy density of Li−S batteries.
Hence, we attempted to stabilize the cycle performance of Cmicro−meso−S with a relatively high sulfur content (51.2 wt %).
The capacity decay of the Cmicro−meso−S/ Li battery with 3 M LiFSI/DME was due to Li2Sx dissolution caused by a few mesopores and uncoordinated DME molecules.

Some reports have shown that high-concentration electrolytes contain less uncoordinated DME; thus, the Li2Sx dissolution is suppressed.24,45 High-concentration LiFSI/DME above 3.6 M without uncoordinated DME would realize Cmicro−meso−S/Li batteries with high energy density and high cycle stability.
Figure 4a shows the charge−discharge curves of Li−S batteries with Cmicro−meso−S cathodes and various concentrations of LiFSI/DME electrolytes at the 1st and 50th cycles.
For 3 M LiFSI/DME, two plateaus were observed.
The highpotential plateau, which is related to readily soluble Li2Sx (x = 6−8), disappeared as the concentration of LiFSI increased (Figure S7).

In the case of 3.6 and 4 M LiFSI/DME, nearly all of the DME were coordinated to Li+ because the molar ratios of LiFSI and DME were 1:2 and 1:1.4, respectively.22 Thus, the dissolution of Li2Sx was significantly inhibited and the highpotential plateau disappeared.
To investigate the suppression effect of the electrolytes on Li2Sx dissolution, solutions prepared by mixing each electrolyte and 0.2 M Li2S8/DME at a volume ratio of 3:1 were observed (Figure S8).
As the LiFSI concentration increased, the dark color became lighter.
This color change suggests that soluble Li2Sx (x = 6−8) was transformed into insoluble short-chain Li2Sx.44,46,47 Therefore, a higher electrolyte concentration suppresses the dissolution of Li2Sx.
The morphology of the Li deposition in 3, 3.6, and 4 M LiFSI/DME was observed using SEM (Figure S9).

The deposited lithium had a nodule-like structure with round edges, which is consistent with previously reported results.22 As the electrolyte concentration increased, Li was densely and uniformly deposited.
Nevertheless, a higher concentration of the electrolyte led to significant capacity decay (Figure 4b).

The capacity retentions of 3.6 and 4 M LiFSI/DME, calculated by dividing the discharge capacity at the 50th cycle (82.3 and 161.6 mA h g−1) by the discharge capacity at the 2nd cycle (1578.8 and 1475.4 mA h g−1), were 5.21 and 11.0%, respectively.
Furthermore, the average coulombic efficiencies of 3.6 and 4 M LiFSI/DME were 90.8 and 92.6%, respectively.

This phenomenon at the cathode also induces a non-uniform current distribution at the anode, resulting in a lower coulombic efficiency.

In contrast, at a very low current density (0.02 C), the coulombic efficiency of the Li−S batteries improved with increasing electrolyte concentration because the non-uniform current distribution was mitigated (Figure 4c).
As a result, 3.6 and 4 M LiFSI/ DME showed higher discharge capacities than 3 M LiFSI/ DME.

Thus, the high-concentration LiFSI/DME electrolyte effectively improved the Li deposition morphology and suppressed Li2Sx dissolution; however, its high viscosity reduced the Li−S battery performance at high current densities.
Electrochemical Performance of Cmicro−meso−S Cathode with LiFSI in DME/HFE Electrolyte.
The above results indicate that a suitable electrolyte for lithium−metal anodes and Cmicro−meso−S cathodes requires a low viscosity and high LiFSI concentration.

Diluted electrolytes with HFE have reduced viscosity and localized high concentrations of LiFSI because LiFSI does not dissolve in HFE.24 Herein, 3 M LiFSI/ DME was diluted with HFE to improve the cycling performance at high current densities and suppress Li2Sx dissolution.
Figure 5a shows the charge−discharge curves of the Li−S batteries with Cmicro−meso−S cathodes and 3 M LiFSI in DME/ HFE electrolytes at the 1st and 50th cycles.
A high-potential plateau, which is attributed to the Li2Sx (x = 4−8) formation reaction, was not observed during the discharge of the Li−S batteries with 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE.
Dilution with HFE increased the concentration of LiFSI in DME, which decreased the amount of free DME.
Therefore, the dissolution of Li2Sx was suppressed in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE.

To investigate the suppression effect of 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE on Li2Sx dissolution, a solution prepared by mixing 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE and 0.2 M Li2S8/DME at a volume ratio of 3:1 was observed (Figure S8), and the dark color of Li2S8 changed to yellow because of the presence of Li2Sx (x = 1, 2).47 Thus, dilution with HFE suppresses the dissolution of Li2Sx.
Figure 5b shows the cycle plots of Li−S batteries with Cmicro−meso−S cathodes and 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE electrolytes.

The HFE dilution suppressed the continuous capacity decay of 3 M LiFSI/DME and improved the capacity retention rate, calculated by dividing the discharge capacity at the 50th cycle (732.3 and 830.4 mA h g−1) by the discharge capacity at the 2nd cycle (1462.9 and 1347.7 mA h g−1), from 50.0 to 61.6%.
Moreover, the average coulombic efficiency improved from 97.1 to 98.5%.
This improved cycling performance with HFE dilution was due to the mitigation of the non-uniform current distribution by decreasing the viscosity of the electrolyte (Table 2).
Furthermore, the decreased viscosity provided 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE with superior performance at high current density (Figure 5c).
The electrochemical performance of Li−S batteries under practical conditions is discussed in the Supporting Information (Figure S10).
Effect of HFE Dilution on Lithium−Metal Anode.
As noted above, HFE dilution suppressed the non-uniform current distribution and Li2Sx dissolution from the cathode.
Herein, the effect of HFE dilution on lithium anodes was investigated.
The SEM images of the lithium anodes after 10 cycles are shown in Figure S9.
The Li metal deposition morphology was dense and uniform upon dilution with HFE, which was also observed for high-concentration LiFSI/DME.
Figure 6a shows the XPS profile of the Li anode after 10 cycles.
The S 2p spectra of Li in 3 M LiFSI/DME and 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE exhibited a peak above 166 eV, which was assigned to the SOx species produced by the decomposition of LiFSI.22,48,49 In Figure 5.

The amount of fluorine on the lithium surface was low (∼0.7 at. %) after dilution with HFE in all the sputtering processes.

Furthermore, the surface of Li in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE had more Li0 than that in 3 M LiFSI/ DME at a sputtering time of 2.4−23 min.53,54 Therefore, the depth profile suggests that the SEI on Li in 3 M LiFSI in DME/HFE is thinner than that in 3 M LiFSI/DME because of the suppression of FSI−decomposition on the Li anode by HFE dilution.

However, it has been reported that HFE dilution of high-concentration LiFSI/DME facilitates the decomposition of FSI−; thus, LiF is enriched.55,56 Our results contradict those of previous studies because the amount of HFE in the electrolyte was lower than that reported in previous studies.

If the HFE ratio is high in the electrolyte, that is, the local concentration is high, FSI−coordinated to Li+ increases, resulting in the formation of an LiF-rich SEI due to the decomposition of FSI−.

The electrolyte used in this study contains a high percentage of DME, which prevents significant anionic decomposition.57 ■CONCLUSIONS In this study, we investigated porous carbon as a sulfur host and the electrolyte composition suitable for Li−S batteries with high-concentration LiFSI/DME.

For improved energy density and stable cycle performance, micro−mesoporous carbon, which contains mesopores with high sulfur content and micropores for the suppression of Li2Sx dissolution, was adopted as the cathode.

S-2 Preparation of porous carbon–sulfur composites Three commercial porous carbons with different pore size distributions (Cmicro, Cmicro-meso, and Cmeso) were used.
Cmicro, Cmicro-meso, and Cmeso were mixed with sulfur (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Co., > 99%) at weight ratios of 76:24 (Cmicro:S), 46:54 (Cmicro-meso:S), and 40:60 (Cmeso:S).
The mixtures were sealed in a stainlesssteel container and heated at 155°C for 5 h under air.
Thus, Cmicro-S, Cmicro-meso-S, and Cmeso-S were obtained.

The sulfur distribution in porous carbons was determined using the following formula: theoretical sulfur content ratio [%] = Vtotal × dLi2S × (MS/MLi2S) [Vtotal× dLi2S × (MS/MLi2S)] + 1 × 100 where Vtotal represents the total pore volume of porous carbons, dLi2S the density of Li2S (1.66 g cm3), Ms the molar mass of sulfur (32.065 g mol−1), and MLi2S the molar mass of Li2S (46.947 g mol−1).
The reason for adding 1 to the denominator is that it is assumed that sulfur is composited with 1 g of carbon.
The sulfur confinement to the porous carbons using the ratio calculated in this formula matches the volume of Li2S produced during discharge with the total pore volume of the porous carbons.
Thus, this sulfur distribution is the theoretical sulfur content ratio that accounts for sulfur expansion during the charge–discharge process.
In the case of Cmicro-meso, the theoretical sulfur content ratio was calculated using more accurate total pore volumes provided by the supplier.
